label: database-row-insert-300-rows
closes: the question of whether the row write is O(rows)
notes: Run at 300 iterations specifically to decide whether to keep optimizing.
It says stop, and it contradicts the extrapolation that motivated it.
THE WRITE IS FLAT. mutate's last quarter is 72ms here, against 67ms in the
40-row run — from ~40 rows to ~300 rows the write did not grow. The
projected '1.4s at 1000 rows' was wrong: it linearly extrapolated a curve
measured only over 0-40 rows, and the curve does not stay linear.
Inside this run mutate goes 130ms (first quarter) -> 72ms (last), a growth
ratio of 0.55. It gets FASTER as the table grows, which is only sensible
once you see what changes partway through: 204 of 300 rows never entered
the DOM. The grid virtualizes, so past roughly 96 rows a newly created row
is no longer rendered, and the per-insert cost of rendering it disappears.
That is the missing ~24ms the in-handler measurement could not account
for: it was client rendering, being attributed to the write because the
scenario stamps a request's end time inside its fetch `.then()` callback,
which a busy main thread delays. The 0-40 row window happened to be
exactly the window where every inserted row still paints.
The one thing that genuinely grows with the table is the read-back:
query goes 9ms -> 43ms (4.87x). It is the only real slope left and 43ms at
300 rows is not a problem worth chasing.
rowInsertMaxMs of 3058ms is a single outlier; p50 is 146ms and there were
zero timeouts across 300 samples.
Integrity: 300/300 samples, 0 timeouts, visible tab, timerClamp 82ms,
measurementTrustworthy true, fresh database, vault holding 3 records.
Caveat for anyone comparing: rowInsertMedianMs is not comparable across
different iteration counts, because sample i is an insert into a table of
size i. Compare last-quarter values at a stated table size instead.
